title: When should EV/EBITDA be used?
subtitle: The preferred ratio when comparing companies with different capital structures
openingQuestion: Why do M&A analysts usually prefer EV/EBITDA over P/E when comparing companies for a merger or acquisition?
openingOptions: Because EBITDA is always more accurate than Net Income
Because EV/EBITDA always gives a higher result than P/E
Because EV/EBITDA doesn't require any debt data
Because EV/EBITDA strips out the effect of capital structure (different debt/equity ratios) and depreciation policy, allowing a 'fairer' comparison between companies with different financial leverage
explanation: EV/EBITDA = Enterprise Value / EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization). Because both EV and EBITDA are 'neutral' to capital structure (unaffected by how much a company borrows, or which depreciation method it uses), this ratio allows a fairer comparison between companies with different financial leverage or accounting policies - especially useful in M&A.

diagram.label: Calculate enterprise value: market cap plus debt minus cash
Both numerator and denominator are independent of capital structure
Lets you compare two companies with different debt levels and depreciation

realWorldExample.description: When comparing two telecom companies - one using heavy debt to invest in infrastructure, the other using equity capital - EV/EBITDA gives a fairer comparison than P/E, since P/E is distorted by the different interest expense between the two companies.

quiz.question: Companies A and B have the same EBITDA, but A carries heavy debt while B has almost none. Whose P/E tends to be more distorted, even though their core operations are equivalent?
options: Company B's, because having no debt gives it higher after-tax profit than A
Can't tell without knowing which industry the two companies are in
Both P/Es are always equal if their EBITDAs are equal
Company A's - large interest expense lowers Net Income and EPS, pushing P/E up
quiz.explanation: This is exactly why EV/EBITDA is preferred over P/E when comparing companies with different capital structures: P/E is affected by interest expense (which sits below the EBITDA line), while EV/EBITDA is not.

quiz.question: A company has EV/EBITDA = 20x while the industry average is only 10x. Besides the company possibly being overvalued, what other reasonable explanation could account for a multiple twice as high?
options: There's no other reasonable explanation besides the company being overvalued
A multiple higher than the industry is always a sign of financial fraud
Possibly outstanding EBITDA growth, a strong moat, or being an M&A target
This company's EV/EBITDA must have been calculated wrong somewhere
quiz.explanation: Comparing a multiple against the industry average is only a starting point - a company with superior quality (higher growth, a durable competitive advantage, lower risk) deserves a higher multiple.

quiz.question: Market cap 2,000 billion, debt 600 billion, cash 100 billion, EBITDA 350 billion. What is EV/EBITDA?
options: 5.7x (= 2,000 ÷ 350, ignoring debt and cash)
quiz.explanation: EV = 2,000 + 600 − 100 = 2,500 billion, divided by EBITDA of 350 gives 7.1x. Debt is added because the buyer has to take it on; cash is subtracted because the buyer gets to keep it.

quiz.question: What is EBITDA's biggest blind spot?
options: It ignores the cost of replacing assets to sustain the business
It's affected by capital structure the same way net profit is
It can only be calculated for a company already listed
It changes according to each country's tax rate
quiz.explanation: Adding back depreciation makes a trucking company that constantly replaces its vehicles look identical to a software company. Charlie Munger called EBITDA earnings before all the expenses that are real - a well-placed warning.

quiz.question: EV/EBITDA 20x versus an industry average of 10x. What should you check before concluding it's expensive?
options: The number of shares outstanding compared with the industry average
Growth rate and profit margin compared against competitors
The dividend policy the business is currently applying to shareholders
The point in time the business first listed on the exchange
quiz.explanation: A multiple double the average could really be expensive, or it could be a fair price for a business growing three times as fast with a much higher margin. Only when growth and margin are comparable but the multiple is still double is that a genuine sign of mispricing.

keyTakeaways: Neutral to capital structure and depreciation policy - suited to comparing companies with different leverage
Widely favored in M&A valuation and cross-industry comparison

practicePrompt.question: A company has Enterprise Value = 8,000 billion, EBITDA = 800 billion. What is this company's EV/EBITDA, and in what situation is this ratio especially more useful than P/E?
options: EV/EBITDA = 8,000/800 = 10x, which is useful when the companies being compared carry different capital structures
EV/EBITDA = EBITDA / Enterprise Value = 800/8,000 = 0.1x, calculated by reversing the standard formula
EV/EBITDA should only be used when a company has absolutely no debt in its capital structure
EV/EBITDA always gives the exact same result as P/E, so the two can be used interchangeably in every case
practicePrompt.explanation: EV/EBITDA = Enterprise Value / EBITDA = 8,000/800 = 10x. This ratio is favored in M&A valuation and cross-industry comparison because it's neutral to capital structure and depreciation policy, allowing a fairer comparison between companies with different debt levels.

summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: Neutral to capital structure and depreciation policy - suited to comparing companies with different leverage

application.title: Apply it now
application.message: Compare two companies in the same industry but with different debt levels using both P/E and EV/EBITDA - observe whether EV/EBITDA gives a 'fairer' result than P/E.
application.secondary: This is the best way to feel for yourself why M&A professionals favor this ratio.

sections.text: When two companies have identical core operations but one carries heavy debt while the other has almost none, their P/Es will diverge even though the underlying business is the same. EV/EBITDA was made exactly to solve this problem.
Why EV/EBITDA is neutral to capital structure

EV/EBITDA = Enterprise Value / EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization). Both the numerator (EV includes debt) and the denominator (EBITDA is calculated before interest) are 'neutral' to how a company chooses to finance itself. If company A borrows heavily and B has almost no debt, but both have equal EBITDA - A's Net Income will be lower than B's due to its larger interest expense, distorting A's P/E (usually higher) even though core operations are equivalent. EV/EBITDA avoids this distortion entirely.
A higher-than-industry multiple isn't automatically mispricing

A company with EV/EBITDA = 20x while the industry average is only 10x isn't necessarily overvalued. The company might have outstanding expected EBITDA growth, a stronger competitive moat, or be priced by the market as a potential M&A target carrying a control premium. Always look for the REASON behind a multiple gap before concluding it's right or wrong.

items: EV/EBITDA suits comparing companies with different financial leverage in the same industry
Unaffected by depreciation policy (accounting differences between companies)
Widely favored in M&A valuation because it reflects the value of the entire business
A multiple higher than the industry average needs an explanation, not a rushed conclusion of 'expensive'

lines: When capital structure muddies P/E, EV/EBITDA is the tool that lets you compare apples to apples.

sections.title: Putting numbers in to see when the multiple breaks

example.title: Two businesses on 8x, very different capital intensity
example.calculation: Software: EBITDA VND 100bn, CapEx 5bn · Factory: EBITDA 100bn, CapEx 70bn · both EV 800bn
example.result: EBITDA − CapEx: software 95bn, factory 30bn → EV/(EBITDA−CapEx) is 8.4x against 26.7x
example.explanation: Both are 8x on EBITDA, but the factory has to hand back 70% of that cash just to keep capacity. EBITDA adds depreciation back - an estimate of real wear - so for a capital-heavy business it omits exactly the largest cost. That is why EV/EBITDA compares businesses of SIMILAR capital intensity well and misleads badly across them.
